Introduction

Card fraud is becoming more prevalent with the current climate or e-commerce and the shifting of the US banking legacy systems over to more cloud based real time transactions. This increases the need for a more robust way to identify transaction fraud. Randon forest has been seen as a way to try to combat this current issue. Research lies in trying to find a way to deal with the unbalanced nature of fraudulent transactions. Less than 2 percent of all transactions are fraudulent so this requires a model that can handle unbalanced data in real time. Most research looks at creating models that can handle this. This paper will look at the common methods and validate their performance against a nonadjusted random forest model. In this paper we are going to test some of the common random forest models against the original algorithm to test if these different models have a greater accuracy impact.

Literature Review

In Random Forest Algorithm Overview, Salman et al. (2024) provide an in-depth review of the benefits and uses of the random forest model, which is a predictive machine learning model. The basis of the model is that it creates decision trees from subsets of data. Having more trees reduces variance. Important features of RF are that they are highly accurate, are rarely overfitted, and can handle data with missing values. Although RF has a lot of advantages, a major constraint of the tool is its inability to produce results efficiently in real-time due to reduced prediction speed after training.

Theory of Random Forests indicates that RF is the most widely adopted machine learning tool due to its versatility for handling various problems as well as computational efficiency. The mathematical theory of RF has lagged even though the tool is highly popular and widely used (Scornet & Hooker, 2026). Random forests were initially created to run classification and regression tests but have expanded into other domains. By altering how the data is reflected in the model, researchers have brought RF into other domains like survival analysis and quantile regression. Research on quantifying RF output has also increased. The central limit theorem and variance of RF are products of the forest’s subsampling that give researchers a way of quantifying the uncertainty of the model’s output (Scornet & Hooker, 2026).

Impact of an improved random forest-based financial management model on the effectiveness of corporate sustainability decisions - ScienceDirect

This article gives an example of how they used a random forest model to help with sustainability decision making in business and to use it as a better early warning sign for a potential financial crisis. They chose to use the random forest model due to its low complexity, resistance to noise data, and good classification performance while also not increasing the computational effort to much. Then they decided how to prune the decision trees to be able to reduce the complexity of the model. They also took their data and normalized it creating Z scores for each data point to make sure each variable would be treated correctly. They were able to create the model to have 98.03% accuracy for predicting financial crisis for companies.

The need for real-time and practical fraud detection systems is challenging due to the volume of credit card transactions processed. Credit fraud, and fraud in general, can have negative impacts that are not limited to financial losses but also include reputational damage from negative consumer experience.

A recent study (Borketey, 2024) compared several machine learning models including but not limited to Logistic Regression, Linear Discriminant Analysis, K-nearest Neighbor, Classification and Regression Trees and others to try to find the best model to use for real-time fraud detection. Borketey used a data set with significant imbalance (0.17% fraudulent transactions). The models were evaluated by using AUC, PRAUC, F1, KS, Recall and Precision. The data set used was not a full representation of global credit card fraud since it was specific to European card issuers. A major limitation is that credit card fraud is always evolving and this may result in models becoming less effective over time. The study found the Random Forest model was the best performing with 71% overall fraud detection.

With the increasing e-commerce transactions, it is important for financial institutions to develop robust fraud detection and with Random Forests being a main tool for real-time fraud detection it is important to understand its strengths and weaknesses. Xuan et al. (2018) compared two random forest variants Random-Tree-Based Random Forest (Random Forest I) and Cart-Based Random Forest (Random Forest II).

This experiment looked at how the two models performed, the ratio of fraudulent to legal transactions, and their performance on a large dataset. The experiment used a data set from a Chinese e-commerce company that was imbalanced and had 0.27% fraudulent transactions. Due to the data imbalance an under-sampling method was used with the Cart-Based Random Forest to test the ratio of legal and fraudulent transactions. The test found that the 5:1 ratio provided the best F-Measure for finding true fraudulent transactions. When this model was tested on a large data set (4.7 million legal and 38,000 fraudulent transactions) to simulate real world scenarios the model had a 33% precision rate. In conclusion, the authors found that RF is good for smaller data sets; however, further research will be required for real world application.

Data-set imbalance can be a real concern when it comes to developing models to detect credit card fraud since these transactions are very small population for processed transactions. Galar et al. (2012) ran a series of experiments to provide a taxonomy and running comparisons to understand how different models handle class imbalance. They used AUC, which provides a single measurement to evaluate the performace of a model, compared to accuracy, because it does not distinguish between the different classifiers. They used a single tree algorithim (C4.5) as the base classifier. The study reviewed 22 ensemble variants across four ensemble groups.

The authors  found that the most complex approaches did not always have the best performance. The most robust methods were SMOTEBagging, RUSBoost, and UnderBagging. They also took into account the complexity of the methods and concluded that RUSBoost provided good performance despite being the least complex. While all ensembles were tested using the C4.5 classifier it is unclear if these results would remain if tested against a different base classifier like a Random Forest.

Manual review of fraudulent credit card transaction is arduous and impractical in today’s financial climate with e-commerce and cross-border payments. Fraudsters’ tactics are constantly changing, and this increases the difficulty of identifying and classifying fraudulent transactions. Fraudulent transactions are a small subset of all processed transactions resulting in a major data imbalance (Aburbeian & Ashqar, 2023). The authors used a modified Random Forest that included synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) to train the model. The authors provide the dataset as 94,682 transactions with 87,562 nonfraud (97.7%) and 2,052 (2.3%) fraudulent, causing an inconsistency in sample calculations. Through testing they found that accuracy is not the best measure of the model and used a confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1 score, and Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC). The random forest classifier accurately classified 98% of the transactions. They found that using SMOTE and hyperparameters provided the more accurate model for addressing the data imbalance with fraudulent transactions. This experiment relied heavily on synthetic data so performance might not directly translate to real-world application.

Methods

The common non-parametric regression model is \(Y_i = m(X_i) + \varepsilon_i\), where \(Y_i\) can be defined as the sum of the regression function value \(m(x)\) for \(X_i\). Here \(m(x)\) is unknown and \(\varepsilon_i\) some errors. With the help of this definition, we can create the estimation for local averaging i.e. \(m(x)\) can be estimated with the product of \(Y_i\) average and \(X_i\) is near to \(x\). In other words, this means that we are discovering the line through the data points with the help of surrounding data points. The estimation formula is printed below (R Core Team 2019):

\[M_n(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} W_n (X_i) Y_i \tag{1}\] \(W_n(x)\) is the sum of weights that belongs to all real numbers. Weights are positive numbers and small if \(X_i\) is far from \(x\).

Another equation:

\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 +\varepsilon_i\]
